claim: MSTN−/− pigs were generated using TALEN genome editing technique with 2 and 4 bp deletions in the two alleles of the MSTN gene.
source: We used MSTN−/− pigs with 2 and 4 bp deletions in the two alleles of the MSTN gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) that were generated using the TALEN genome editing technique (Kang et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication (Kang et al., 2017) as the source for the generation method and provides genetic sequence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have higher skeletal muscle mass compared to wild-type pigs.
source: We found that MSTN−/− pigs had higher skeletal muscle mass and myofiber cross-sectional area (CSA) but a lack of MSTN expression and lower phosphorylation of Smad2/3 in skeletal muscle (Figure 1A−C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and measurements shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have larger myofiber cross-sectional area compared to wild-type pigs.
source: We found that MSTN−/− pigs had higher skeletal muscle mass and myofiber cross-sectional area (CSA) but a lack of MSTN expression and lower phosphorylation of Smad2/3 in skeletal muscle (Figure 1A−C).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs lack MSTN expression in skeletal muscle.
source: We found that MSTN−/− pigs had higher skeletal muscle mass and myofiber cross-sectional area (CSA) but a lack of MSTN expression and lower phosphorylation of Smad2/3 in skeletal muscle (Figure 1A−C).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 1C shows absence of MSTN protein in MSTN−/− pigs.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have lower phosphorylation of Smad2/3 in skeletal muscle compared to wild-type pigs.
source: We found that MSTN−/− pigs had higher skeletal muscle mass and myofiber cross-sectional area (CSA) but a lack of MSTN expression and lower phosphorylation of Smad2/3 in skeletal muscle (Figure 1A−C).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 1C demonstrates reduced p-Smad2/3 levels.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have significantly higher protein expression of MyHC type IIb in skeletal muscle.
source: In addition, the protein expression of myosin heavy chain (MyHC) type IIb; MyoD; and glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1 and PKM2 was significantly higher in skeletal muscle (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1C shows increased MyHC IIb protein levels.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have significantly higher protein expression of MyoD in skeletal muscle.
source: In addition, the protein expression of myosin heavy chain (MyHC) type IIb; MyoD; and glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1 and PKM2 was significantly higher in skeletal muscle (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1C shows increased MyoD protein levels.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have significantly higher protein expression of glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1 and PKM2 in skeletal muscle.
source: In addition, the protein expression of myosin heavy chain (MyHC) type IIb; MyoD; and glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1 and PKM2 was significantly higher in skeletal muscle (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1D shows increased levels of these glycolytic enzymes.

claim: The ACE alpha-diversity index was significantly lower in MSTN−/− pigs compared to wild-type pigs.
source: The ACE of MSTN−/− pigs was significantly lower than that of the WT pigs, but there were no difference in the Chao 1, Shannon, and Simpson indexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B−E).
evidence: Statistical analysis of microbiota diversity shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MSTN deficiency causes a reduction in the diversity of the intestinal microbiota.
source: These results suggest that MSTN deficiency causes a reduction in the diversity of the intestinal microbiota.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ACE index data showing lower diversity in MSTN−/− pigs.

claim: The composition of the gut microbiota differs between MSTN−/− and wild-type pigs.
source: The composition of the gut microbiota, was analyzed using principal components analysis (PCA), which showed that the two groups can be clearly differentiated (Figure 1E).
evidence: PCA analysis in Figure 1E shows clear separation between the two groups.

claim: Romboutsia is significantly more abundant at the genus level in MSTN−/− pigs compared to wild-type pigs.
source: LEfSe analysis confirmed a significant difference at the genus level with respect to Romboutsia (Figure 1F). In addition, Treponema, Romboutsia, and Turicibacter, all of which produce SCFAs (Kreznar et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019b; Li et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019c ; Bian et al., 2020), were significantly more abundant at the genus level in MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 1G).
evidence: LEfSe analysis in Figure 1F and abundance data in Figure 1G demonstrate increased Romboutsia.

claim: Treponema, Romboutsia, and Turicibacter produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs).
source: In addition, Treponema, Romboutsia, and Turicibacter, all of which produce SCFAs (Kreznar et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019b; Li et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019c ; Bian et al., 2020), were significantly more abundant at the genus level in MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Treponema is significantly more abundant at the genus level in MSTN−/− pigs compared to wild-type pigs.
source: In addition, Treponema, Romboutsia, and Turicibacter, all of which produce SCFAs (Kreznar et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019b; Li et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019c ; Bian et al., 2020), were significantly more abundant at the genus level in MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 1G).
evidence: Abundance data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Turicibacter is significantly more abundant at the genus level in MSTN−/− pigs compared to wild-type pigs.
source: In addition, Treponema, Romboutsia, and Turicibacter, all of which produce SCFAs (Kreznar et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019b; Li et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019c ; Bian et al., 2020), were significantly more abundant at the genus level in MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 1G).
evidence: Abundance data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have a thicker intestinal muscularis compared to wild-type pigs.
source: We observed the muscularis was thicker and the plicae were longer and the expression of the smooth muscle proteins α-SMA and calponin-1 was higher in MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Histological measurements shown in Figure 2A demonstrate increased muscularis thickness.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have longer intestinal plicae compared to wild-type pigs.
source: We observed the muscularis was thicker and the plicae were longer and the expression of the smooth muscle proteins α-SMA and calponin-1 was higher in MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Histological measurements shown in Figure 2A demonstrate increased plica length.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have higher expression of smooth muscle proteins α-SMA and calponin-1 in the intestine.
source: We observed the muscularis was thicker and the plicae were longer and the expression of the smooth muscle proteins α-SMA and calponin-1 was higher in MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2C shows increased protein levels.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have higher expression of tight junction-related genes TJP1 and OCLN in the intestine.
source: In addition, the expression of the tight junction-related genes TJP1 and OCLN was higher (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 2B and protein data in Figure 2D.

claim: Intestinal tight junctions are regulated by MLCK and MLC.
source: Intestinal tight junctions are regulated by MLCK and MLC (Sinpitaksakul et al., 2008; Chun et al., 2014), and we found that the levels of MLCK and p-MLC were decreased in the intestine of MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have decreased levels of MLCK and p-MLC in the intestine.
source: Intestinal tight junctions are regulated by MLCK and MLC (Sinpitaksakul et al., 2008; Chun et al., 2014), and we found that the levels of MLCK and p-MLC were decreased in the intestine of MSTN−/− pigs (Figure 2D).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2D shows decreased MLCK and p-MLC levels.

claim: Treatment of IPEC-J2 cells with MSTN receptor inhibitor SB431542 reduces MLCK and p-MLC levels.
source: IPEC-J2 cells treated with the inhibitor of MSTN receptor SB431542 caused a reduction in MLCK and p-MLC levels, thereby inducing high expression of the tight junction factors TJP1 and OCLN (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2E shows reduced MLCK and p-MLC after SB431542 treatment.

claim: Treatment of IPEC-J2 cells with MSTN receptor inhibitor SB431542 induces high expression of tight junction factors TJP1 and OCLN.
source: IPEC-J2 cells treated with the inhibitor of MSTN receptor SB431542 caused a reduction in MLCK and p-MLC levels, thereby inducing high expression of the tight junction factors TJP1 and OCLN (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Gene expression data in Figure 2F shows increased TJP1 and OCLN after SB431542 treatment.

claim: MSTN gene deletion affects intestinal barrier function through the MLCK/MLC pathway.
source: These results demonstrate that MSTN gene deletion affects intestinal barrier function through the MLCK/MLC pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing reduced MLCK/p-MLC and increased tight junction proteins.

claim: Mice transplanted with MSTN−/− pig feces (KO-M) have higher muscle mass than mice transplanted with WT pig feces (WT-M).
source: After 8 weeks of normal chow feeding, the KO-M had higher muscle mass than the WT-M and, in particular, large gastrocnemius (GA) muscles (Figure 3A).
evidence: Muscle mass measurements shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: KO-M mice have significantly larger gastrocnemius (GA) muscle mass compared to WT-M mice.
source: The GA mass, but not that of the soleus (SOL) or extensor digitorum longus (EDL), was significantly larger in the KO-M than in the WT-M (Figure 3B).
evidence: Muscle mass measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There were no significant differences in food intake between KO-M and WT-M mice.
source: However, there were no significant differences in the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed of the two mouse groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A−E).
evidence: Food intake data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There were no significant differences in physical activity between KO-M and WT-M mice.
source: However, there were no significant differences in the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed of the two mouse groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A−E).
evidence: Physical activity data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There were no significant differences in energy intake between KO-M and WT-M mice.
source: However, there were no significant differences in the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed of the two mouse groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A−E).
evidence: Energy intake data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There were no significant differences in energy absorbed between KO-M and WT-M mice.
source: However, there were no significant differences in the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed of the two mouse groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A−E).
evidence: Energy absorbed data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: KO-M mice have larger myofiber cross-sectional areas in gastrocnemius muscle compared to WT-M mice.
source: Quantitative analysis of the fiber size of the GA muscles revealed that the fibers were hypertrophic, and that the distribution of fiber size was shifted toward larger fibers in the KO-M (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: KO-M mice have larger cross-sectional areas of type IIb myofibers compared to WT-M mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, the CSAs of type IIb myofibers of the KO-M were larger than those of the WT-M.
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 3E.

claim: KO-M mice have significantly higher expression of MyHC IIb protein in gastrocnemius muscle compared to WT-M mice.
source: Consistent with this, the expression of the proteins MyHC IIb and MyoD, and of the glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2, was significantly higher in the GA muscles of the KO-M, whereas the expression of MyHC I and IIa did not significantly differ (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3F shows increased MyHC IIb protein levels.

claim: KO-M mice have significantly higher expression of MyoD protein in gastrocnemius muscle compared to WT-M mice.
source: Consistent with this, the expression of the proteins MyHC IIb and MyoD, and of the glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2, was significantly higher in the GA muscles of the KO-M, whereas the expression of MyHC I and IIa did not significantly differ (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3F shows increased MyoD protein levels.

claim: KO-M mice have significantly higher expression of glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2 in gastrocnemius muscle compared to WT-M mice.
source: Consistent with this, the expression of the proteins MyHC IIb and MyoD, and of the glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2, was significantly higher in the GA muscles of the KO-M, whereas the expression of MyHC I and IIa did not significantly differ (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3G shows increased levels of these glycolytic enzymes.

claim: KO-M mice have greater Akt and mTOR phosphorylation in skeletal muscles compared to WT-M mice.
source: There was also greater Akt and mTOR phosphorylation in the skeletal muscles of the KO-M (Figure 3H).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3H shows increased phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR.

claim: The Akt/mTOR signaling pathway causes type IIb myofiber hypertrophy.
source: The Akt/mTOR signaling pathway causes type IIb myofiber hypertrophy (Izumiya et al., 2008; Dutchak et al., 2018), and therefore this may explain the greater GA mass in the KO-M.
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: KO-M mice have higher grip force compared to WT-M mice.
source: Consistent with the expression profile of type IIb myofibers, the grip force of the KO-M was higher than that of the WT-M (Figure 3I).
evidence: Grip strength measurements shown in Figure 3I.

claim: KO-M mice have lower running capacity compared to WT-M mice.
source: However, the KO-M mice had a lower running capacity (Figure 3J).
evidence: Running time measurements shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Type IIb myofibers are responsible for explosive force rather than endurance.
source: These findings may be explained by enlargement in the type IIb myofibers, a type of fast-twitch glycolytic muscle, which are responsible for explosive force rather than endurance.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about muscle fiber types.

claim: The composition of the intestinal microbiota differs between KO-M and WT-M mice.
source: Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) showed that the composition of the intestinal microbiota of the two groups clearly differed (Figure 4A).
evidence: PCoA analysis in Figure 4A shows clear separation between the two groups.

claim: The genus Romboutsia is significantly enriched in the intestines of KO-M mice.
source: In addition, the genus Romboutsia and the corresponding family and order Peptostreptococcaceae and Peptostreptococcales-Tissierellales were significantly enriched in the intestines of the KO-M (Figure 4B).
evidence: Microbiota abundance data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Romboutsia, which was upregulated in MSTN−/− pigs, was also upregulated in KO-M mice.
source: Romboutsia, which was upregulated in MSTN−/− pigs, was also upregulated in the KO-M (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Comparative microbiota data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Intestinal microbial functions of KO-M mice are dominated by pathways related to the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites.
source: Functional prediction analysis showed that intestinal microbial functions of the KO-M were dominated by pathways related to the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites (Figure 4E).
evidence: Functional prediction analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SCFAs are metabolites of the intestinal microbiota that can affect the growth and function of skeletal muscle.
source: SCFAs are metabolites of the intestinal microbiota that can affect the growth and function of skeletal muscle (Frampton et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: SCFAs are present at higher concentrations in the colonic contents of KO-M mice compared to WT-M mice.
source: Analysis of the fatty acid composition of the colonic contents of the mice showed that SCFAs were present at higher concentrations in the KO-M than in the WT-M.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Valeric acid and isobutyric acid are present at significantly higher concentrations in the colonic contents of KO-M mice compared to WT-M mice.
source: In particular, valeric acid and isobutyric acid were present at significantly higher concentrations in the KO-M (Figure 5A).
evidence: Fatty acid analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There were no differences in the concentrations of medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) between KO-M and WT-M mice.
source: However, there were no differences in the concentrations of medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) (Figure 5B) or in the concentration of long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) between the two groups (Figure 5C).
evidence: Fatty acid analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There were no differences in the concentrations of long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) between KO-M and WT-M mice.
source: However, there were no differences in the concentrations of medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) (Figure 5B) or in the concentration of long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) between the two groups (Figure 5C).
evidence: Fatty acid analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Valeric acid treatment increases myotube diameter in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Immunofluorescence staining for MyHC showed that after supplementation with valeric acid, the C2C12 myoblasts produced thicker myotubes and showed a higher fusion index than the control cells, which implies that valeric acid promotes myotube formation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Valeric acid treatment increases myotube fusion index in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Immunofluorescence staining for MyHC showed that after supplementation with valeric acid, the C2C12 myoblasts produced thicker myotubes and showed a higher fusion index than the control cells, which implies that valeric acid promotes myotube formation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Valeric acid promotes myotube formation in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Immunofluorescence staining for MyHC showed that after supplementation with valeric acid, the C2C12 myoblasts produced thicker myotubes and showed a higher fusion index than the control cells, which implies that valeric acid promotes myotube formation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increases in myotube diameter and fusion index.

claim: Valeric acid treatment increases the expression of MyoD and MyoG in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Valeric acid treatment also increased the expression of MyoD and MyoG and promoted the differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts (Figure 6B).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6B shows increased MyoD and MyoG protein levels.

claim: Valeric acid treatment promotes the differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Valeric acid treatment also increased the expression of MyoD and MyoG and promoted the differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on increased expression of differentiation markers MyoD and MyoG.

claim: Valeric acid treatment significantly increases the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: In addition, the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR was significantly higher following valeric acid treatment (Figure 6C).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6C shows increased phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR.

claim: Isobutyric acid only increases the myotube fusion index in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: However, isobutyric acid did not have all of these effects, and it only increased the myotube fusion index.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Valeric acid can promote myogenic differentiation of myoblasts.
source: Taken together, these results strongly demonstrate that valeric acid can promote myogenic differentiation of myoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including increased myotube formation, MyoD/MyoG expression, and Akt/mTOR activation.

claim: Valeric acid treatment significantly increases the mass of gastrocnemius (GA) muscles in mice.
source: Mice were administered valeric acid (100 mg/kg) daily by oral gavage, which significantly increased the masses of the GA muscles, a fast-twitch glycolytic skeletal muscle, versus the control muscles (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Muscle mass measurements shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Valeric acid treatment increases the cross-sectional areas of gastrocnemius muscle fibers in mice.
source: Consistently, valeric acid treatment caused an increase in the CSAs of the GA muscle and in the proportion of large myofibers (Figure 7C).
evidence: Histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Valeric acid treatment increases the proportion of large myofibers in gastrocnemius muscle.
source: Consistently, valeric acid treatment caused an increase in the CSAs of the GA muscle and in the proportion of large myofibers (Figure 7C).
evidence: Histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Valeric acid treatment significantly increases the expression of glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2 in gastrocnemius muscle.
source: Furthermore, valeric acid treatment significantly increased the expression of the glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2 (Figure 7E); the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR in the GA muscle (Figure 7F); and the grip force of the mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7E shows increased levels of these glycolytic enzymes.

claim: Valeric acid treatment significantly increases the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR in gastrocnemius muscle.
source: Furthermore, valeric acid treatment significantly increased the expression of the glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2 (Figure 7E); the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR in the GA muscle (Figure 7F); and the grip force of the mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7F shows increased phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR.

claim: Valeric acid treatment significantly increases the grip force of mice.
source: Furthermore, valeric acid treatment significantly increased the expression of the glycolytic enzymes HK2, PFK1, and PKM2 (Figure 7E); the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR in the GA muscle (Figure 7F); and the grip force of the mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: Grip strength measurements shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Valeric acid treatment increases the length of the small intestine in mice.
source: Interestingly, valeric acid treatment also increased the length of the small intestine (Figure 7H) but had no effect on the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed by the mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Intestinal length measurements shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Valeric acid treatment has no effect on food intake in mice.
source: Interestingly, valeric acid treatment also increased the length of the small intestine (Figure 7H) but had no effect on the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed by the mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Food intake data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Valeric acid treatment has no effect on physical activity in mice.
source: Interestingly, valeric acid treatment also increased the length of the small intestine (Figure 7H) but had no effect on the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed by the mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Physical activity data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Valeric acid treatment has no effect on energy intake in mice.
source: Interestingly, valeric acid treatment also increased the length of the small intestine (Figure 7H) but had no effect on the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed by the mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Energy intake data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Valeric acid treatment has no effect on energy absorbed in mice.
source: Interestingly, valeric acid treatment also increased the length of the small intestine (Figure 7H) but had no effect on the food intake, physical activity, energy intake, or energy absorbed by the mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Energy absorbed data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Valeric acid treatment increases the mRNA expression of FFAR2 in gastrocnemius muscle.
source: Valeric acid increased the mRNA expression of FFAR2 in GA muscle, whereas that of FFAR3 and HCAR2 was not affected (Figure 7I).
evidence: Real-time PCR data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Valeric acid treatment does not affect the mRNA expression of FFAR3 and HCAR2 in gastrocnemius muscle.
source: Valeric acid increased the mRNA expression of FFAR2 in GA muscle, whereas that of FFAR3 and HCAR2 was not affected (Figure 7I).
evidence: Real-time PCR data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: GPR43 inhibitor GLPG0974 prevents valeric acid-induced increases in skeletal muscle mass.
source: Next, mice were orally administered the GPR43-specific inhibitor GLPG0974, which prevented the valeric acid-induced increases in skeletal muscle mass and fiber hypertrophy (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Muscle mass measurements shown in Figure 8A.

claim: GPR43 inhibitor GLPG0974 prevents valeric acid-induced fiber hypertrophy.
source: Next, mice were orally administered the GPR43-specific inhibitor GLPG0974, which prevented the valeric acid-induced increases in skeletal muscle mass and fiber hypertrophy (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Valeric acid activates AKT and mTOR via GPR43 in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Consistent with this, the results of FFAR2 knockdown in C2C12 myoblasts confirmed that valeric acid activates AKT and mTOR via GPR43 (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: FFAR2 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8C and D demonstrate that valeric acid effects are mediated through GPR43.

claim: Acetic acid and propionic acid do not increase the expression of FFAR2 in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: We also compared the effect of valeric acid on myogenic differentiation with that of acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid, and found that acetic acid and propionic acid did not increase the expression of FFAR2, whereas butyric acid and valeric acid significantly increased the mRNA expression of FFAR2 and the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR, and only valeric acid induced high expression of MyoD and MyoG (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: Real-time PCR data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Butyric acid and valeric acid significantly increase the mRNA expression of FFAR2 in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: We also compared the effect of valeric acid on myogenic differentiation with that of acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid, and found that acetic acid and propionic acid did not increase the expression of FFAR2, whereas butyric acid and valeric acid significantly increased the mRNA expression of FFAR2 and the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR, and only valeric acid induced high expression of MyoD and MyoG (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: Real-time PCR data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Butyric acid and valeric acid increase the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: We also compared the effect of valeric acid on myogenic differentiation with that of acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid, and found that acetic acid and propionic acid did not increase the expression of FFAR2, whereas butyric acid and valeric acid significantly increased the mRNA expression of FFAR2 and the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR, and only valeric acid induced high expression of MyoD and MyoG (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Only valeric acid induces high expression of MyoD and MyoG among the tested SCFAs in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: We also compared the effect of valeric acid on myogenic differentiation with that of acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid, and found that acetic acid and propionic acid did not increase the expression of FFAR2, whereas butyric acid and valeric acid significantly increased the mRNA expression of FFAR2 and the phosphorylation of Akt and mTOR, and only valeric acid induced high expression of MyoD and MyoG (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Valeric acid induces type IIb/glycolytic myofiber growth by activating Akt/mTOR signaling via GPR43.
source: These findings suggest that valeric acid induces type IIb/glycolytic myofiber growth and increases GA mass by activating Akt/mTOR signaling via GPR43.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including GPR43 inhibition studies and FFAR2 knockdown experiments.

claim: Glucocorticoids such as dexamethasone are often used experimentally to induce muscle atrophy.
source: Glucocorticoids, such as dexamethasone (Dex), are often used experimentally to induce muscle atrophy and are known to influence protein metabolism in skeletal muscle, and high levels are considered to be a risk factor for the development of muscle atrophy (Hong et al., 2019; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: High levels of glucocorticoids are considered to be a risk factor for the development of muscle atrophy.
source: Glucocorticoids, such as dexamethasone (Dex), are often used experimentally to induce muscle atrophy and are known to influence protein metabolism in skeletal muscle, and high levels are considered to be a risk factor for the development of muscle atrophy (Hong et al., 2019; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Valeric acid administration ameliorates skeletal muscle atrophy induced by dexamethasone in mice.
source: Valeric acid administration ameliorated the skeletal muscle atrophy induced by Dex in mice and reduced the dissolution area with a clear morphology of muscle fiber (Figure 9A).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 9A demonstrates reduced muscle damage.

claim: Valeric acid significantly reduces the mRNA and protein expression of atrogin-1 and MuRF-1 induced by dexamethasone.
source: It also significantly reduced the mRNA and protein expression of the pro-atrophic factors atrogin-1 and MuRF-1, the expression of which was induced by Dex (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: Western blot and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: Valeric acid treatment significantly increases myotube diameter in dexamethasone-treated C2C12 myoblasts.
source: In C2C12 myoblasts, valeric acid treatment significantly increased myotube diameter and fusion index, and reduced the expression of the pro-atrophic factors, thereby ameliorating the Dex-induced myotube atrophy (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Valeric acid treatment significantly increases myotube fusion index in dexamethasone-treated C2C12 myoblasts.
source: In C2C12 myoblasts, valeric acid treatment significantly increased myotube diameter and fusion index, and reduced the expression of the pro-atrophic factors, thereby ameliorating the Dex-induced myotube atrophy (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Valeric acid ameliorates dexamethasone-induced myotube atrophy in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: In C2C12 myoblasts, valeric acid treatment significantly increased myotube diameter and fusion index, and reduced the expression of the pro-atrophic factors, thereby ameliorating the Dex-induced myotube atrophy (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed increases in myotube diameter and fusion index and reduced expression of atrophic factors.

claim: Valeric acid ameliorates dexamethasone-induced muscle atrophy.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that valeric acid ameliorates Dex-induced muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both in vivo and in vitro experimental observations.

claim: Host genetic variations can influence the composition of gut microbiota.
source: Host genetic variations can influence the composition of gut microbiota, and the gut microbiota can affect skeletal muscle growth and function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: The gut microbiota can affect skeletal muscle growth and function.
source: Host genetic variations can influence the composition of gut microbiota, and the gut microbiota can affect skeletal muscle growth and function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: The gut microbiota was changed by MSTN gene deletion in pigs.
source: In the present study, we found that the gut microbiota was changed by MSTN gene deletion in pigs, and that the transplantation of this intestinal microbiota promotes skeletal muscle hypertrophy in mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings supported by the microbiota analysis data presented earlier.

claim: Transplantation of intestinal microbiota from MSTN−/− pigs promotes skeletal muscle hypertrophy in mice.
source: In the present study, we found that the gut microbiota was changed by MSTN gene deletion in pigs, and that the transplantation of this intestinal microbiota promotes skeletal muscle hypertrophy in mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings supported by the FMT experiment data presented earlier.

claim: This is the first study to show that MSTN knockout leads to changes in intestinal morphology.
source: The present study is the first to show that MSTN knockout leads to a loss of expression in the intestine, which was associated with a thicker intestinal muscularis and longer plicae in the pigs, indicating that MSTN knockout induces changes in intestinal morphology.
evidence: The authors claim novelty based on their experimental observations.

claim: MSTN deletion alters the intestinal barrier through the MLCK/p-MLC pathway.
source: Importantly, we have shown for the first time that MSTN gene deletion alters the intestinal barrier through the MLCK/p-MLC pathway, which would be expected to affect the composition of intestinal microbiota.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing reduced MLCK/p-MLC and increased tight junction proteins.

claim: The intestinal microbiota remodeled by MSTN gene deletion increases fast-twitch glycolytic muscle growth through an increase in the production of valeric acid.
source: Furthermore, we have provided evidence that the intestinal microbiota remodeled by MSTN gene deletion increases fast-twitch glycolytic muscle growth through an increase in the production of valeric acid, which activates the Akt/mTOR pathway through the SCFA receptor GPR43.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including FMT, SCFA analysis, and valeric acid treatment studies.

claim: Valeric acid activates the Akt/mTOR pathway through the SCFA receptor GPR43.
source: Furthermore, we have provided evidence that the intestinal microbiota remodeled by MSTN gene deletion increases fast-twitch glycolytic muscle growth through an increase in the production of valeric acid, which activates the Akt/mTOR pathway through the SCFA receptor GPR43.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from GPR43 inhibition and FFAR2 knockdown experiments.

claim: Valeric acid has a beneficial effect on skeletal muscle atrophy induced by dexamethasone.
source: Finally, we have shown that valeric acid has a beneficial effect on the skeletal muscle atrophy induced by Dex (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dexamethasone-induced atrophy experiments.

claim: MSTN regulates myogenic differentiation and skeletal muscle mass principally by activating classical Smad2/3 transcription factors.
source: MSTN regulates myogenic differentiation and skeletal muscle mass principally by activating classical Smad2/3 transcription factors (Chen et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs exhibit stronger muscle hypertrophy and fiber enlargement, showing a significant 'double-muscle' phenotype.
source: MSTN−/− pigs exhibit stronger muscle hypertrophy and fiber enlargement, showing a significant 'double-muscle' phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the experimental data presented earlier.

claim: The degree of increased muscle mass and fiber size in mice after fecal microbiota transplantation is limited compared to MSTN-KO pigs.
source: However, the degree of increased muscle mass and fiber size in mice after fecal microbiota transplantation is limited, with only significant increase observed in type IIb muscle fibers.
evidence: This is an observation comparing the phenotypes between MSTN-KO pigs and FMT mice.

claim: The autonomous changes in muscle cells induced by MSTN KO may be its primary pathway for muscle hypertrophy.
source: Therefore, the phenotype of increased skeletal muscle mass in mice is not as significant as that in MSTN-KO pigs. We believe that the autonomous changes in muscle cells induced by MSTN KO may be its primary pathway, and our results strongly support the important role of MSTN-mediated changes in gut microbiota in skeletal muscle hypertrophy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative results between MSTN-KO pigs and FMT mice.

claim: MSTN expression has been identified in smooth muscle of blood vessels, penis, and other tissues where it co-localizes with α-smooth muscle actin.
source: MSTN expression has been identified not only in skeletal muscles but also in the smooth muscle of blood vessels, the penis, and other tissues, where it co-localizes with α-smooth muscle actin and can affect organ function (Verzola et al., 2017; Esposito et al., 2020; Kovanecz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: MSTN expression in intestine has been demonstrated.
source: Intestine also contains smooth muscle, and MSTN expression in intestine has been demonstrated; however, its role in the intestine is unclear (Sundaresan et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The muscularis is important for intestinal motility, and its thickness relates to the peristaltic ability of the intestine.
source: The muscularis is important for intestinal motility, and its thickness relates to the peristaltic ability of the intestine.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The height of the mucosal fold determines the surface area available for intestinal absorption.
source: In addition, the height of the mucosal fold determines the surface area available for intestinal absorption (Wang et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2017; Geda et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: MSTN−/− pigs have greater intestinal absorptive capacity.
source: The identified increases in small intestinal muscularis thickness and plical length imply that MSTN−/− pigs have greater intestinal absorptive capacity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increases in muscularis thickness and plical length.

claim: Tight junctions between adjacent intestinal epithelial cells are a critical component of the intestinal barrier.
source: Tight junctions between adjacent intestinal epithelial cells are a critical component of the intestinal barrier (Ghosh et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: A disruption in the intestinal barrier leads to greater entry of bacterial products into the circulation, which triggers an inflammatory response in specific tissues.
source: Previous studies have shown that a disruption in the intestinal barrier leads to greater entry of bacterial products, including lipopolysaccharide, into the circulation, which triggers an inflammatory response in specific tissues, such as skeletal muscle and adipose tissue (Ghosh et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Intestinal barrier function is regulated by the MLCK/MLC pathway.
source: Intestinal barrier function is regulated by the MLCK/MLC pathway (Sinpitaksakul et al., 2008; Chun et al., 2014), and interestingly, the expression of MLCK and the phosphorylation of MLC were significantly lower in MSTN−/− pigs.
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: MSTN may regulate intestinal tight junction function in pigs through the MLCK/MLC pathway.
source: These results suggest that MSTN may regulate intestinal tight junction function in pigs through the MLCK/MLC pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in MLCK/MLC and tight junction proteins.

claim: The IPEC-J2 cell line has morphological and functional similarities to porcine intestinal cells.
source: The IPEC-J2 cell line has morphological and functional similarities to porcine intestinal cells, and it therefore represents a good model for the assessment of intestinal barrier function (Brosnahan and Brown, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Inhibition of the MSTN receptor causes down regulation of MLCK and p-MLC and improves tight junctions of IPEC-J2 cells.
source: We found that inhibition of the MSTN receptor caused down regulation of MLCK and p-MLC and improved the tight junctions of IPEC-J2 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the experimental data in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The deletion of the MSTN gene in the intestine can affect the intestinal environment through the MLCK/MLC pathway.
source: Therefore, we believe that the deletion of the MSTN gene in the intestine can affect the intestinal environment through the MLCK/MLC pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the IPEC-J2 cell experiments and the observations in MSTN−/− pigs.

claim: Changes in the intestinal environment and barrier function can alter the microbial composition of the gut.
source: Importantly, changes in the intestinal environment and barrier function can alter the microbial composition of the gut (Seganfredo et al., 2017; Nicoletti et al., 2017; Sekirov et al., 2010; Tremaroli et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Romboutsia and Turicibacter are closely associated with metabolic disorders such as hypertension, diabetes, dysregulation of skeletal muscle energy metabolism, and obesity.
source: In addition, Romboutsia (Li et al., 2021; Yanni et al., 2020) and Turicibacter (Watanabe et al., 2021) are closely associated with metabolic disorders, such as hypertension, diabetes, the dysregulation of skeletal muscle energy metabolism, and obesity.
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Alterations in intestinal structure and barrier function induced by MSTN gene deletion may affect the composition of the intestinal microbiota.
source: Therefore, the alterations in intestinal structure and barrier function induced by the deletion of the MSTN gene in the intestine may affect the composition of the intestinal microbiota.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed changes in intestinal structure, barrier function, and microbiota composition.

claim: Fecal microbiota transplantation can lead to the transfer of both the host gut characteristics and metabolic phenotype from pigs to mice.
source: FMT can lead to the transfer of both the host gut characteristics and metabolic phenotype from pigs to mice (Yang et al., 2018; Diao et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Akt1 transgene activation specifically increases gastrocnemius mass and type IIb myofiber size through an mTOR-dependent pathway.
source: Previous studies have shown that Akt1 transgene activation specifically increases GA mass and type IIb myofiber size through an mTOR-dependent pathway (Izumiya et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Augmentation of type IIb myofiber is associated with an increase in grip strength but a reduction in endurance during treadmill testing.
source: In addition, augment of type IIb myofiber was associated with an increase in grip strength but a reduction in endurance during treadmill testing (Izumiya et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Treatment with the microbial metabolite SCFAs ameliorates impairments in skeletal muscle by increasing MyoD expression and reducing atrogin-1 expression.
source: Moreover, previous research has shown that treatment with the microbial metabolite SCFAs also ameliorates impairments in skeletal muscle, and especially in the GA muscle, by increasing MyoD expression and reducing atrogin-1 expression (Lahiri et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: In C2C12 cells, SCFAs stimulate mitochondrial respiration and promote a switch of energy production mode from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolytic.
source: In C2C12 cells, SCFAs also stimulates mitochondrial respiration and promotes a switch of energy production mode from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolytic (Lahiri et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The intestinal microbiota associated with MSTN gene deletion causes growth of fast-twitch glycolytic muscle and improves function.
source: These results strongly suggest that the intestinal microbiota associated with MSTN gene deletion causes a growth of fast-twitch glycolytic muscle and improves function, which may be mediated by the enrichment of SCFA-producing microbes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FMT experiments and SCFA analysis.

claim: SCFAs are the principal metabolites generated by the intestinal microbiota and are involved in multiple physiological processes in the host.
source: SCFAs are the principal metabolites generated by the intestinal microbiota and are involved in multiple physiological processes in the host (Donohoe et al., 2011; Canfora et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Acetic acid improves mitochondrial metabolism and promotes the formation of oxidative muscle fibers.
source: We observed that valeric acid treatment increases myotube formation in myoblasts, and increases the mass of GA muscles and type IIb muscle fiber size in mice; meanwhile, in previous studies, acetic acid has been shown to improve mitochondrial metabolism and promote the formation of oxidative muscle fibers (Pan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: SCFAs play a regulatory role principally by binding to GPR41, GPR43, and GPR109a.
source: SCFAs play a regulatory role principally by binding to GPR41, GPR43, and GPR109a (Stoddart et al., 2008; Van Hul and Cani, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Aging and long-term or high-dose glucocorticoid therapy induce skeletal muscle atrophy, which principally manifests as a loss of skeletal muscle mass with a relatively selective loss of type IIb muscle fibers.
source: Aging and long-term or high-dose glucocorticoid therapy induce skeletal muscle atrophy, which principally manifests as a loss of skeletal muscle mass, with a relatively selective loss of type IIb muscle fibers (Akasaki et al., 2014; Haber and Weinstein, 1992; Faulkner et al., 2007; Kirkendall and Garrett, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: This is the first study to identify the MSTN gene-gut microbiota-SCFA axis and its regulatory role in fast-twitch glycolytic muscle growth.
source: This is the first study to identify the MSTN gene-gut microbiota-SCFA axis and its regulatory role in fast-twitch glycolytic muscle growth.
evidence: The authors claim novelty for their comprehensive findings linking MSTN, gut microbiota, and SCFAs in muscle growth regulation.

claim: The deletion of the myostatin (MSTN) gene positively regulates the expression of the intestinal tight junction-related genes TJP1 and OCLN through the myosin light-chain kinase/myosin light chain pathway.
source: In this study, we found that the deletion of the myostatin (MSTN) gene positively regulates the expression of the intestinal tight junction-related genes TJP1 and OCLN through the myosin light-chain kinase/myosin light chain pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The intestinal structure of MSTN−/− pigs differed from wild-type, including by the presence of a thicker muscularis and longer plicae.
source: The intestinal structure of MSTN−/− pigs differed from wild-type, including by the presence of a thicker muscularis and longer plicae.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by histological data in Figure 2A.

claim: Changes in intestinal structure affect the structure of intestinal microbiota.
source: Together, these changes affect the structure of intestinal microbiota.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the observed changes in intestinal structure and microbiota composition.

claim: Mice transplanted with the intestinal microbiota of MSTN−/− pigs had myofibers with larger cross-sectional areas.
source: Mice transplanted with the intestinal microbiota of MSTN−/− pigs had myofibers with larger cross-sectional areas and higher fast-twitch glycolytic muscle mass.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Mice transplanted with the intestinal microbiota of MSTN−/− pigs had higher fast-twitch glycolytic muscle mass.
source: Mice transplanted with the intestinal microbiota of MSTN−/− pigs had myofibers with larger cross-sectional areas and higher fast-twitch glycolytic muscle mass.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Microbes responsible for the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were enriched in both the MSTN−/− pigs and recipient mice.
source: Microbes responsible for the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were enriched in both the MSTN−/− pigs and recipient mice, and SCFAs levels were elevated in the colon contents.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by microbiota analysis in Figures 1 and 4, and SCFA measurements in Figure 5.

claim: SCFAs levels were elevated in the colon contents of mice transplanted with MSTN−/− pig microbiota.
source: Microbes responsible for the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were enriched in both the MSTN−/− pigs and recipient mice, and SCFAs levels were elevated in the colon contents.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by SCFA measurements in Figure 5.

claim: Valeric acid stimulates type IIb myofiber growth by activating the Akt/mTOR pathway via G protein-coupled receptor 43.
source: We also demonstrated that valeric acid stimulates type IIb myofiber growth by activating the Akt/mTOR pathway via G protein-coupled receptor 43 and ameliorates dexamethasone-induced muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Valeric acid ameliorates dexamethasone-induced muscle atrophy.
source: We also demonstrated that valeric acid stimulates type IIb myofiber growth by activating the Akt/mTOR pathway via G protein-coupled receptor 43 and ameliorates dexamethasone-induced muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 9.
